Linear Data Structures

Linear data structures store elements in a sequence. The four workhorses are arrays, linked lists, stacks, and queues. Choosing the right one shapes how fast your code runs.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

An array is like numbered lockers in a row: if you know the number you jump straight to it. A linked list is like a scavenger hunt where each clue points to the next — you must follow the chain.

An array stores elements in one contiguous block of memory, so element i is found with simple pointer arithmetic in O(1). A linked list stores each element in a node that holds a pointer to the next node; nodes can be scattered anywhere in memory.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Arrays give O(1) random access but O(n) insertion in the middle (elements must shift). Linked lists give O(1) insertion once you hold the node, but O(n) access because you must walk from the head.

A stack is Last-In-First-Out (LIFO): push adds to the top, pop removes the top. Function call frames use a stack. A queue is First-In-First-Out (FIFO): enqueue at the back, dequeue at the front — like a print job line.

📝 KEY IDEA

Match the structure to the access pattern: contiguous indexed access → array; frequent front/middle insertions → linked list; undo/backtracking → stack; scheduling/buffering → queue.

Example: a text editor's undo feature pushes each edit onto a stack; pressing undo pops the most recent edit first. A web server's request buffer is a queue so requests are served in arrival order.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Assuming linked lists are always faster for insertion. In practice arrays often win due to cache locality — contiguous memory is prefetched, while chasing scattered node pointers causes cache misses.

Trees, Heaps & Hash Tables

Beyond linear structures, three hierarchical/associative structures dominate: trees, heaps, and hash tables. They trade a little complexity for much faster search and priority operations.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A hash table is a coat check: you hand over a coat and get a ticket number computed from it. Later that number sends you straight to the right hook — no searching the whole rack.

A binary search tree (BST) keeps smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right. A balanced BST supports search, insert, and delete in O(log n). A heap is a complete binary tree where every parent is ≤ (min-heap) or ≥ (max-heap) its children; the extreme element is always at the root.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

A hash table applies a hash function to a key to compute an index into an array of buckets. On average lookups are O(1). Collisions (two keys hashing to the same bucket) are resolved by chaining (a list per bucket) or open addressing (probing for the next slot).

Example: a priority queue built on a min-heap always dequeues the smallest key first — used by Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm and by task schedulers. Python's dict and set are hash tables.

📝 KEY IDEA

Use a BST or balanced tree when you need sorted order and range queries; use a heap when you only need repeated access to the min or max; use a hash table for fast unordered key lookups.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Assuming hash tables are always O(1). With a poor hash function or adversarial keys, many collisions can degrade lookups to O(n).

Graph Algorithms

A graph is a set of vertices connected by edges. Graphs model networks, dependencies, maps, and neural-network computation graphs. Two traversals are fundamental: BFS and DFS.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

BFS explores like ripples spreading from a stone dropped in water — all nearby nodes first. DFS is like exploring a maze by following one corridor to its end before backtracking.

Breadth-first search uses a queue and visits vertices in order of distance from the start. On an unweighted graph it finds the shortest path (fewest edges). Depth-first search uses a stack (or recursion) and dives deep before backtracking; it is used for cycle detection and topological sorting.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

For weighted graphs with non-negative weights, Dijkstra's algorithm uses a min-priority-queue (min-heap) to repeatedly expand the closest unsettled vertex, producing shortest paths in about O((V+E) log V) time.

Example: finding the fewest connections between two friends in a social network uses BFS. Finding the cheapest driving route where roads have different lengths uses Dijkstra. If edges can be negative, Bellman-Ford is needed instead.

📝 KEY IDEA

Unweighted shortest path → BFS. Non-negative weighted shortest path → Dijkstra. Ordering tasks with dependencies → DFS-based topological sort.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Using plain BFS for weighted graphs. BFS counts edges, not weights, so it can return a path with fewer edges but greater total cost.

📊 FIGURE — choosing a graph representation
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — The space difference on a realistic graph

Take a social graph with V = 100,000 users and about 50 friends each, so E ≈ 2,500,000 edges.

  • Adjacency matrix: V² = 10,000,000,000 cells — ten billion, almost all of them zero.
  • Adjacency list: V + 2E = 100,000 + 5,000,000 ≈ 5,100,000 entries.

That is roughly 1,960× less space, and it is why the answer is sparse: a list wins whenever E is small relative to V².

The trade is lookup. \"Are u and v adjacent?\" is O(1) in a matrix but O(deg u) in a list. Choose by which question you ask most.

🎯 EXAM TIP
An adjacency list is preferred when the graph is sparse — its O(V + E) space beats the matrix's unconditional O(V²). Real graphs (social networks, road maps, web links) are almost always sparse, which is why lists are the default in practice.

Dynamic Programming & Greedy Algorithms

Both techniques solve optimization problems, but they think differently. Dynamic programming (DP) breaks a problem into subproblems, solves each once, and reuses the answers. Greedy algorithms make the locally best choice at each step and never reconsider.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

DP is like keeping a notebook of answers you've already worked out so you never redo the same calculation. Greedy is like always grabbing the biggest coin at hand, hoping it adds up to the best total.

DP applies when a problem has overlapping subproblems (the same smaller problems recur) and optimal substructure (an optimal solution is built from optimal subsolutions). Naive Fibonacci recomputes values exponentially; DP stores them and runs in O(n).

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Two DP styles: memoization is top-down recursion that caches results; tabulation is bottom-up, filling a table from base cases upward. Both convert exponential recursion into polynomial time by eliminating recomputation.

Example: computing the 40th Fibonacci number naively makes over a billion calls; with memoization it makes about 40. The coin-change minimum-coins problem needs DP because greedy fails for some coin sets (e.g. coins 1, 3, 4 making 6).

📝 KEY IDEA

Use greedy only when a greedy-choice property is proven (e.g. Huffman coding, Dijkstra). When local choices can trap you in a suboptimal path, use DP.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Assuming greedy always works. For coin sets like {1,3,4} making 6, greedy picks 4+1+1 (three coins) while the optimum is 3+3 (two coins).

📊 FIGURE — LCS, and what \"subsequence\" means
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — LCS of ABCBDAB and BDCABA

Filling the DP table gives a final value of 4. Two different subsequences achieve it — BCBA and BDAB — which is normal: the length is unique, the subsequence itself need not be.

Check BCBA by hand against both strings:

  • A B C B D A B — picks positions 2, 3, 4, 6
  • B D C A B A — picks positions 1, 3, 5, 6

The letters appear in the same order in both, with gaps allowed. That gap-tolerance is exactly what separates a subsequence from a substring — the longest common substring here is only length 2.

🎯 EXAM TIP
The LCS of ABCBDAB and BDCABA is 4. Keep subsequence and substring apart: a subsequence keeps only the order and may skip characters, a substring must be contiguous. Nearly every trap in this topic is that distinction.

Complexity Analysis (Big-O)

Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's running time or memory grows as input size n grows. It ignores constants and lower-order terms to focus on scalability — what matters when n is large.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Big-O is like asking 'how does the drive time grow as the trip gets longer?' not 'exactly how many minutes.' A highway (O(n)) scales gently; a route that revisits every town pairwise (O(n²)) blows up.

Common classes from fastest to slowest: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic, O(n) linear, O(n log n) linearithmic, O(n²) quadratic, O(2ⁿ) exponential. Binary search is O(log n); a single loop is O(n); a nested loop over the same data is O(n²).

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

To analyze code, count how the number of basic operations scales with n, keep only the dominant term, and drop constant factors. So 3n + 5 is O(n), and n²/2 + n is O(n²).

Example: doubling the input of an O(n) algorithm roughly doubles its time; doubling the input of an O(n²) algorithm roughly quadruples it. This is why an O(n²) sort becomes unusable on large datasets while O(n log n) sorts scale.

📝 KEY IDEA

When comparing algorithms for large inputs, the complexity class dominates. An O(n log n) algorithm beats an O(n²) one for large n even if the O(n²) one has smaller constants.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Confusing Big-O with actual speed on small inputs. For tiny n, a simpler O(n²) method can beat an O(n log n) one; Big-O describes asymptotic growth, not fixed runtime.

📊 FIGURE — the three things asked here
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why 2T(n/2) + O(n) is n log n, and why 1024 takes 10 halvings

The recurrence. Draw the recursion tree. Each level splits the work in half but there are twice as many pieces, so every level does O(n) total combining work. The tree is log₂n levels deep, so the total is

O(n) × log₂n = O(n log n)

This is exactly the merge sort recurrence. Change the combine step to O(1) and the total collapses to O(n); recurse only once instead of twice and you get O(log n), which is binary search.

The halvings. 1024 → 512 → 256 → 128 → 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1. Counting the arrows gives 10, because 2¹⁰ = 1024. That count is log₂n, which is why binary search over 1024 sorted items needs about 10 comparisons.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Three facts from this section. The fastest-growing of the usual classes is O(n²). T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) is O(n log n) — recognise it as merge sort. And halving 1024 down to 1 takes 10 steps, because log₂1024 = 10.

Operating Systems & Memory Management

The operating system (OS) is the software layer between hardware and applications. Its kernel manages the CPU, memory, and devices, and enforces isolation between programs.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Virtual memory is like giving every tenant their own apartment numbering that starts at 1, while the building manager secretly maps those to real rooms. Tenants never clash even though they use the same 'address'.

Each process runs in its own virtual address space. The OS, with hardware (the MMU), translates virtual addresses to physical RAM using paging: memory is divided into fixed-size pages that can be mapped, swapped to disk, or shared. This gives isolation and the illusion of more memory than physically exists.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Programs request OS services (files, memory, I/O) through system calls, which switch from unprivileged user mode to privileged kernel mode. This boundary prevents a buggy program from corrupting the whole machine.

Within a process, the stack holds function locals and grows/shrinks automatically with calls; the heap holds dynamically allocated memory that the program (or a garbage collector) must manage. Example: training a large model that exceeds RAM triggers heavy paging to disk, drastically slowing training — a real systems concern in AI.

📝 KEY IDEA

Virtual memory + paging is why many processes can coexist safely and why an app can address more memory than the machine physically has.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Assuming a memory address in one process points to the same physical location in another. Virtual addresses are per-process; identical numbers usually map to different physical memory.

Processes, Threads & Concurrency

A process is an independent program with its own memory space. A thread is a lightweight unit of execution inside a process; threads of the same process share memory. Concurrency lets a program make progress on multiple tasks.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A process is a separate kitchen with its own ingredients. Threads are several cooks in the same kitchen sharing the same counters — fast to coordinate, but they can collide reaching for the same knife.

Because threads share memory, two threads updating the same variable can interleave badly — a race condition. A lock (mutex) forces one thread at a time into a critical section, restoring correctness at the cost of some serialization.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Concurrency means tasks are in progress in overlapping time; parallelism means tasks literally run at the same instant on multiple cores. You can have concurrency on one core via time-slicing, but true parallelism needs multiple cores.

Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, so CPU-bound Python threads don't run in parallel. For CPU-bound work, use multiprocessing or native libraries (NumPy, PyTorch) that release the GIL and use C/GPU under the hood. Example: a data-loading pipeline uses threads for I/O overlap while heavy matrix math runs in GIL-releasing native code.

📝 KEY IDEA

Use threads for I/O-bound overlap and processes (or native/GPU kernels) for CPU-bound parallelism, especially in Python.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Expecting Python threads to speed up CPU-bound loops. The GIL serializes bytecode, so such threads compete rather than parallelize; use multiprocessing instead.

📊 FIGURE — why counter += 1 is not atomic
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — How an increment gets lost

Trace two threads with the counter at 41:

  • Thread A reads 41
  • Thread B reads 41  ← before A has written
  • Thread A computes 42, writes 42
  • Thread B computes 42, writes 42

Two increments happened; the counter advanced by one. That is a lost update.

With two threads doing 1000 increments each, the answer is some value between 2 and 2000. 2000 is the best case (no interleaving); the theoretical worst case is 2, because each thread's final write still lands. Anything in between is possible, and the value changes from run to run — which is what makes these bugs so hard to reproduce.

The fix is to make read-modify-write indivisible: hold a lock around it, or use an atomic increment.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE
Assuming the answer is \"always 2000, just slower\" or \"a random number near 2000\". Neither is right. The guarantee is only that the result lies between 2 and 2000, and in practice you often see something close to 2000 — which is worse than an obvious failure, because the bug hides in testing and surfaces under load.

Distributed Computing

Distributed computing spreads work across many networked machines. It is essential when data or computation exceeds a single machine — exactly the case for training large AI models.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A distributed system is like a restaurant kitchen with many stations. Output soars when stations work in parallel, but everything depends on messages between them — a lost ticket or a slow station stalls the meal.

Horizontal scaling (adding more machines) handles growth that a single bigger machine cannot. Data is partitioned (sharded) across nodes, and computation is coordinated over the network. The hard parts are partial failures, network latency, and keeping data consistent.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

The CAP theorem states that during a network partition a distributed store must trade off between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a response). You cannot have both when the network splits.

Example: training a large language model uses data parallelism — each GPU/node processes a different batch of data with a copy of the model, then gradients are averaged across nodes (an all-reduce) each step. Communication bandwidth between nodes often becomes the bottleneck, which is why fast interconnects matter as much as raw compute.

📝 KEY IDEA

Distributed AI training is limited not only by compute but by the network cost of synchronizing gradients across nodes each step.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Assuming adding nodes always speeds things up linearly. Communication and synchronization overhead grows, so doubling nodes rarely halves training time.

Languages for AI: Python, C++, SQL

AI engineering leans on a small set of languages, each for a different job: Python for productivity, C++ for performance, and SQL for data.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Python is the friendly control room where you flip switches and read dashboards. C++/CUDA is the roaring engine room below deck doing the heavy lifting. SQL is the warehouse clerk who fetches exactly the crates you ask for.

Python is dominant because it is concise, has a vast ecosystem (NumPy, PyTorch, TensorFlow), and reads almost like pseudocode — ideal for fast experimentation. But pure Python is slow, so the heavy math is delegated.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Frameworks like PyTorch expose a Python API but execute tensor operations in optimized C++ and CUDA kernels on the GPU. You get Python's ease with near-native speed because the inner loops never run as interpreted Python bytecode.

C++ gives manual memory control and predictable performance, so it underlies these frameworks and production inference engines. SQL is the language of relational databases, used to query, join, filter, and aggregate the training data that lives in data warehouses.

📝 KEY IDEA

The winning pattern is 'Python on top, C++/CUDA underneath': write clear high-level code that calls into fast compiled kernels.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Writing performance-critical inner loops in pure Python. Interpreted loops are far slower than vectorized calls into NumPy/PyTorch, which run compiled native code.

📊 FIGURE — GROUP BY and the aggregate
🎯 EXAM TIP
The shape is SELECT label, COUNT(*) FROM data GROUP BY label. Without GROUP BY the aggregate collapses the entire table into a single row. And remember which filter goes where: WHERE removes rows before grouping, HAVING removes groups after — \"only labels with more than 100 rows\" is a HAVING.

CPUs, GPUs & the Memory Hierarchy

A CPU has a few powerful cores optimized for low latency — finishing one complex task quickly. A GPU has thousands of simpler cores optimized for throughput — doing many similar operations at once, ideal for the matrix math in neural networks.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A CPU is a few expert chefs each cooking an elaborate dish fast. A GPU is a thousand line cooks all chopping vegetables simultaneously — unbeatable when the job is the same simple operation repeated a million times.

The memory hierarchy trades speed for capacity. From fastest/smallest to slowest/largest: registers, L1/L2/L3 cache, main memory (RAM/GPU VRAM), then disk. Each level down is larger but much slower.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Data must be near the compute units to be useful. When a core needs data not in cache, it stalls waiting for slower memory. Keeping frequently used data in fast caches is what makes real hardware fast, not just raw core count.

Neural-network training is dominated by matrix multiplications, which map perfectly onto a GPU's many cores. But feeding those cores is hard: models and activations must stream from VRAM. When arithmetic units wait on memory, the workload is memory-bandwidth bound. Example: many transformer inference steps are limited by how fast weights can be read from memory, not by raw FLOPs.

📝 KEY IDEA

GPUs win AI workloads because neural nets are massively parallel; but performance often hinges on memory bandwidth, not just core count or peak FLOPs.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Judging a chip only by peak FLOPs. If memory bandwidth can't feed the cores, real throughput falls far short of the theoretical peak.

Parallel Computing & CUDA

Parallel computing performs many operations simultaneously. GPUs achieve this with a SIMT model — Single Instruction, Multiple Threads — where many threads execute the same instruction on different data.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

CUDA is like conducting a huge choir: you give one instruction ('sing this note') and thousands of voices apply it to their own part at once. Your job is to organize the singers into sections so no one collides.

CUDA is NVIDIA's platform for programming GPUs. Work is organized as a grid of blocks, each block containing many threads. Threads within a block can cooperate via fast shared memory; the runtime schedules blocks across the GPU's streaming multiprocessors.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

A GPU executes threads in groups called warps (32 threads) that run in lockstep. If threads in a warp take different branches (divergence), the paths run serially, wasting parallelism. Well-parallelized code keeps threads doing the same work on adjacent data.

Problems parallelize well when they are data-parallel — the same operation applied independently across many elements, like adding two large vectors or multiplying matrices. Example: a CUDA kernel for element-wise vector addition launches one thread per element, and thousands run concurrently.

📝 KEY IDEA

Neural-network training maps onto CUDA because its heavy operations (matrix multiply, convolutions) are data-parallel and reused across huge tensors.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Heavy branching inside a warp. Thread divergence serializes the branches, so control-flow-heavy code often runs poorly on GPUs compared to CPUs.

📊 FIGURE — what actually limits a small GPU job
🎯 EXAM TIP
A CUDA loop that copies a little data over, launches a tiny kernel and copies back each iteration is limited by PCIe transfer and kernel launch overhead, not GPU arithmetic. The GPU is fast at the maths and slow at being interrupted — so move data once, keep it resident, and batch the work.

Why Compute Limits Modern AI

Modern AI progress is tightly coupled to compute. Larger models trained on more data with more floating-point operations tend to perform better — the observation behind scaling laws. This makes hardware a central bottleneck, not just algorithms.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of training as filling a swimming pool. Compute is the width of your hose, data is the water, and model size is the pool. Bigger pools and more water need a fatter hose and more time — or you wait forever.

Training a frontier model can require thousands of GPUs running for weeks. Three hardware limits dominate: raw FLOPs (arithmetic throughput), memory (a model's parameters and activations must fit in VRAM), and interconnect bandwidth (nodes must synchronize gradients each step).

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

When a model is too large for one GPU's memory, it is split across many GPUs (model/tensor/pipeline parallelism). This introduces communication every step, so the network fabric between GPUs becomes as important as the GPUs themselves.

Cost and energy also cap what is feasible: compute is expensive and power-hungry, so efficiency (better chips, quantization, sparsity) matters as much as scale. Example: doubling model parameters can more than double memory and communication needs, so gains eventually run into a wall of hardware and dollars rather than ideas.

📝 KEY IDEA

AI capability is currently gated by compute, memory, interconnect, and cost — which is why hardware efficiency and parallelization strategy are first-class concerns.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Believing only algorithms limit AI. In practice, memory capacity, interconnect bandwidth, energy, and cost frequently bound what can actually be trained.

Recurrences, Amortization & Hardness

\n
💡 KEY RESULTS

Master theorem for T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n) with critical exponent c*=log_b(a): Case 1 (f=O(n^(c*-e))) gives Θ(n^c*); Case 2 (f=Θ(n^c* log^k n), k≥0) gives Θ(n^c* log^(k+1) n); Case 3 (f=Ω(n^(c*+e)) with regularity af(n/b)≤cf(n), c<1) gives Θ(f(n)). Akra-Bazzi handles unequal splits: find p with Σ a_i b_i^p = 1.

\n
⚙️ FORMULAS

Σ_{i=1}^n i = n(n+1)/2. Geometric Σ r^i = (r^{n+1}-1)/(r-1). T(n)=T(n-1)+f(n) ⇒ Σ f. Amortized: aggregate (total/ops), accounting (credits), potential Φ with ĉ_i=c_i+Φ_i-Φ_{i-1}. Dynamic array doubling ⇒ O(1) amortized push.

\n
📝 TECHNIQUE

Greedy correctness via exchange argument: transform any optimal solution into the greedy one without worsening cost. DP needs optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems; runtime = (#states)×(work/transition). NP-completeness: show in NP (poly verifier) then poly-time reduce a known NPC problem TO it (correct direction).

\n
⚠️ SUBTLETY

Master theorem has a GAP: f between polynomial classes (e.g. f=n/log n, or n^c* log n only fits Case 2 with k≥0). Case 3 REQUIRES the regularity condition. Reduction direction: to prove X is NP-hard, reduce KNOWN-hard→X, not X→known. Amortized O(1) does NOT bound worst-case single op.

📊 FIGURE — when the Master Theorem does not apply
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Solving T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n

The two subproblems have different sizes, so the Master Theorem does not apply. Akra–Bazzi asks for the exponent p satisfying

(1/3)ᵖ + (2/3)ᵖ = 1

Try p = 1: 1/3 + 2/3 = 1. ✓ So p = 1.

The formula then gives T(n) = Θ(nᵖ (1 + ∫₁ⁿ g(u)/u^{p+1} du)) with g(u) = u:

∫₁ⁿ u/u² du = ∫₁ⁿ du/u = ln n

T(n) = Θ(n(1 + ln n)) = Θ(n log n)

The intuition matches: the work per level is still n, and although the tree is lopsided its depth is still logarithmic — the 2/3 branch reaches depth log_{3/2}n.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Reach for Akra–Bazzi when the subproblems are unequal in size, since the Master Theorem requires them equal. Solve Σ aᵢbᵢᵖ = 1 for p first — and for the common uneven splits that sum to the whole input, p = 1 and the answer is Θ(n log n).

Concurrency, Memory Models & Distributed

\n
💡 KEY RESULTS

Coffman's four necessary conditions for deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait — breaking any ONE prevents deadlock. Linearizability: each operation appears to take effect atomically at some point between its invocation and response; it is composable (local). Sequential consistency is NOT composable. CAP: under a network Partition you choose Consistency OR Availability.

\n
⚙️ FORMULAS

A data race = two concurrent accesses, ≥1 write, no happens-before ordering. Lock ordering (total order on locks) prevents circular wait. Consensus needs f+1 rounds to tolerate f crash faults (synchronous); Paxos/Raft need a majority quorum ⌊n/2⌋+1; BFT needs n≥3f+1. False sharing: distinct variables on the same cache line (typically 64 bytes) ping-pong under MESI.

\n
📝 TECHNIQUE

Lock-free progress: at least one thread makes progress system-wide (vs wait-free: every thread in bounded steps). CAS(addr,old,new) is the universal primitive (consensus number ∞). Detect the ABA problem with tagged pointers/hazard pointers. Prove deadlock-freedom by exhibiting a global lock acquisition order.

\n
⚠️ SUBTLETY

volatile in C/C++ does NOT provide atomicity or ordering for concurrency. Linearizability ≠ serializability (transactions). 'Eventual consistency' allows stale reads. Sequential consistency permits reordering that linearizability's real-time constraint forbids. A benign-looking non-atomic read/write pair is still a race and UB under the C11/Java memory model.

Parallelism & GPU Performance Math

\n
💡 KEY RESULTS

Amdahl (fixed problem): S(N)=1/((1-p)+p/N); limit N→∞ is 1/(1-p). Gustafson (scaled problem): S(N)=(1-p)+pN = N−(1-p)(N−1). Roofline: attainable FLOP/s = min(peak compute, peak BW × arithmetic intensity). Ridge point AI = peak_FLOPs/peak_BW separates memory-bound (left) from compute-bound (right).

\n
⚙️ FORMULAS

Arithmetic intensity AI = FLOPs / bytes moved. SAXPY (y=ax+y, fp32): 2 FLOP / 12 B = 1/6. Dot product fp32: 2 FLOP / 8 B = 1/4. Occupancy = active warps / max warps per SM. Ring all-reduce bandwidth term = 2(N−1)/N × D/B; latency term = 2(N−1)α. A warp = 32 threads (lockstep SIMT).

\n
📝 TECHNIQUE

Classify a kernel: compute AI, compare to ridge point. If AI < ridge → memory-bound (optimize coalescing/reuse); if AI > ridge → compute-bound (optimize ILP/tensor cores). Occupancy is limited by the MIN over three caps: registers/thread, shared memory/block, and the hardware thread/warp ceiling per SM.

\n
⚠️ SUBTLETY

Amdahl's serial fraction hard-caps speedup regardless of N. Higher occupancy does NOT guarantee higher throughput (latency hiding can saturate below 100%). Warp divergence serializes branches within a warp. Uncoalesced global loads waste bandwidth. Gustafson looks linear because the serial part stays fixed while work grows.
